en: The Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch Master,
compiled by the monk Zongbao, successor to the patriarchs and abbot of Fengfan Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple.
1. On the first day of the journey, the Great Master arrived at Baolin Temple.

Wei Cishi of Shaozhou, whose name was Ju, together with his officials, entered the mountains to invite the Master. He emerged from the city and, at the lecture hall of Dabian Temple, expounded the Dharma for the assembly, opening the conditions for their awakening.

After the Master ascended the seat, more than thirty provincial governors and officials, more than thirty Confucian scholars and academicians, and over a thousand monks, nuns, and laypeople simultaneously prostrated themselves, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
The Great Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"O virtuous friends!
The self-nature of Bodhi is originally pure; by simply employing this mind, one directly realizes Buddhahood."
"Good friends! Listen to the account of my origins and the circumstances by which I attained the Dharma.
My late father was originally from Fanyang; he was demoted to the region south of the Ling Mountains and became a commoner in Xinzhou."
This body has met with misfortune, and my father passed away prematurely.
Left alone and orphaned by my aged mother, we moved to the South Sea; enduring hardship and poverty, I sell firewood in the marketplace.
At that time, there was a traveler who purchased firewood and sent someone to deliver it to an inn;
once the traveler had taken it away, Huineng received the money and went outside the gate, where he saw another traveler reciting a sutra.
Upon hearing these words from the scripture, Huineng’s mind was immediately enlightened.
He then asked, "What scripture is the guest reciting? The guest replied:
"The Diamond Sutra. He asked again,
"From where have you come, holding this scripture?"
The guest said, "I have come from Dongchan Monastery in Huangmei County, Qizhou.
That monastery was where the Great Master Wuzu Ren presided over the transformation of others; there were more than one thousand disciples."
I went there to pay my respects and listen to this sutra.

The Great Master constantly exhorted both monastics and laypeople that by simply upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one would spontaneously realize one's own nature and directly attain Buddhahood.

Upon hearing these words, Huineng realized he had a karmic affinity from past lives. Thereupon, a guest took ten taels of silver and gave it to him, instructing him to use it for his mother’s clothing and sustenance, and telling him to go immediately to Huangmei to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch.
After Huineng had settled his mother, he immediately took his leave.
In less than thirty days, he arrived at Huangmei to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked:
"From what region do you come?
What do you seek?"
Huineng replied, "I am a commoner from Xinzhou in Lingnan. I have come from afar to pay my respects to the Master; I seek only to become a Buddha, and nothing else."
The Patriarch said, "You are a man from south of the Ling Mountains and, moreover, a hunter; how can you possibly become a Buddha? Huineng replied:
"Although people have distinctions of north and south, the Buddha-nature fundamentally has no such distinction.
Although the bodies of the hunters and the śramaṇa are different, how could there be any difference in their Buddha-nature?"
The Fifth Patriarch wished to speak with him further, but seeing that his disciples were all gathered around, he ordered him to join the assembly in manual labor.
Huineng said, "I, Huineng, inform the Master: within my own mind, wisdom constantly arises; not departing from one's own nature is itself the field of merit."
"I do not yet know what task the Master instructs me to perform.
The Patriarch said,
"This barbarian has a most keen root-nature!"
"Do not speak further; go and work in the barn.
Huineng retreated to the rear courtyard, where an attendant assigned him to split firewood and tread upon the pestle.
After more than eight months had passed, the Patriarch one day suddenly saw Huineng and said:
"I have considered that your insight is worthy of use; however, fearing that malicious people might harm you, I have therefore not spoken with you."
"Do you understand? Huineng replied, "I, your disciple, also understand the Master's intention; I did not dare proceed to the hall so as not to be noticed by others."
One day, the Patriarch called all his disciples together and said:

"I have told you that for worldly beings, the matter of birth and death is of great importance. Yet you spend your days seeking only fields of merit, rather than seeking liberation from the bitter sea of birth and death.
If your own nature is deluded, how can mere merit save you?"
"Go each of you now and examine your own wisdom; grasp the nature of *prajñā* within your own original mind and compose a verse for me to see.
If you have awakened to the great meaning, I shall transmit the robe and the Dharma to you as the sixth patriarch."
Fire departs with extreme rapidity; it cannot be delayed. If one deliberates, it is of no use.
One who perceives their nature must see it in the moment of speech.
If this is so, one may perceive it even while facing an array of whirling blades on the battlefield.
Those of sharp faculties were granted permission by the assembly to withdraw. As they withdrew, they said to one another:
"There is no need for us to clear our minds and exert ourselves to compose verses to present to the Master; what benefit would that bring?"
"The Venerable Shenxiu is currently the Master of Instruction; he must have obtained it.
We have wasted our mental energy composing these verses in vain.
Upon hearing these words, everyone else ceased their efforts and all said:
"We shall henceforth rely upon Master Xiù; why trouble ourselves with composing verses? Shenxiù reflected:
"The reason these people do not present verses is that I am acting as their instructor."
I must compose a verse to present to the Master; for if I do not present a verse, how will the Master know the depth or shallowness of my understanding?

My intention in presenting this verse is that it would be virtuous if I seek the Dharma, yet it would be wrong if I seek the Patriarchate—for what difference is there between such a mind, which is no different from that of an ordinary person, and one that usurps a sacred position?
"If you do not present the verse, you will ultimately not obtain the Dharma.
How great a difficulty!
How great a difficulty!"

"In front of the Hall of the Fifth Patriarch, there were three bays of a covered walkway. It was intended that the court artist Lu Chen be invited to paint the transformation tableaux of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the genealogical chart of the Five Patriarchs, to be circulated for veneration."

After Shenxiu had finished composing the verse, he wished to present it several times; yet as he walked before the hall, his mind became dazed and sweat poured from his entire body, so that he was unable to present it.
Over the course of four days, he attempted to present the verse thirteen times, but failed each time.
Xiu then thought to himself:
"It would be better to write it on the corridor wall so that the Master may see it. If he says it is good, I shall come out and prostrate, saying, 'This was written by Xiu.
But if he says it is unworthy, then all these years spent in the mountains receiving the prostrations of others—what further path could there be to cultivate?"
That night, during the third watch, without letting anyone know, he personally took a lamp and inscribed a verse on the wall of the southern corridor to present what his mind had perceived.
The verse says:
“The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror stand.”
"From time to time, diligently wipe it clean, / And do not let it gather dust.
After Xiu had finished writing this verse, he returned to his room; no one knew of it.
Xiu further reflected:
"If the Fifth Patriarch sees my verse tomorrow and rejoices, then I have a karmic affinity with the Dharma;
if he says I am not capable, it is simply because of my own delusion and heavy past karmic obstructions that prevent me from receiving the Dharma."
The Sage’s intent was difficult to fathom; he remained in his quarters with anxious thoughts, unable to find peace whether sitting or reclining, until the fifth watch of the night.
The Patriarch already knew that Shenxiu had not yet entered the gate nor perceived his own nature.
At dawn, the Patriarch summoned Lu Gongfeng to paint a portrait on the wall of the southern corridor. Suddenly seeing the verse, he said to him, "Gongfeng, there is no need for you to paint;
it was a waste of your coming from so far."
The Sūtra says:
"All that has marks is entirely illusory.
I shall leave only this verse for others to recite and uphold.
"By practicing according to this verse, one may avoid falling into the evil realms;
by practicing according to this verse, there is great benefit.
He then had his disciples light incense and pay their respects, and as they recited this verse in its entirety, they immediately attained the realization of their own nature.
The disciples recited the verse and all exclaimed, "Excellent!
At the third watch, the Patriarch summoned Xiu to enter the hall and asked him, "Is this verse yours?"
Xiu said, "It was indeed composed by Xiu.
I do not dare falsely seek the position of the Patriarch; I only hope that the Master, out of compassion, will examine whether this disciple possesses even a small measure of wisdom."
The Patriarch said:
"By composing this verse, you have not yet seen your original nature; you have merely reached the gate's exterior, but have not yet entered within.
With such an understanding, it is utterly impossible to seek and attain unsurpassed Bodhi."
To attain unsurpassed bodhi, one must recognize one’s own fundamental mind beneath a single word and perceive one’s own original nature as neither arising nor ceasing;

at all times, in every thought-moment, one must personally see that the myriad dharmas are without obstruction—wherein the One is true and all are true, and the myriad objects are as they are in their suchness.
The mind as it truly is (tathatā-citta) is itself reality.
To see it in this way is the very nature of unsurpassed bodhi.
You should go now and reflect for a day or two; compose another verse and bring it here for me to examine.
"If your verse enters the gate, I shall entrust you with the robe and the Dharma.
Shenxiu bowed and departed.

After several more days had passed, he was unable to compose a verse; his mind became hazy and unsettled, his spirit and thoughts were restless, as if in a dream, and he found no joy in either walking or sitting.
Two days later, a young boy passed by the millhouse chanting that verse;
as soon as Huineng heard it, he knew that the verse had not yet revealed the true nature. Although he had not received formal instruction, he already grasped its essential meaning.
He then asked the youth,
"What verse are you reciting?
The youth replied:
"You ignorant hunter do not understand that the Master said:
'The matter of birth and death for those in the world is of great importance; I wish to transmit the robe and the Dharma, so I have had my disciples compose verses for me to examine.'"
"If you awaken to the Great Meaning, I shall immediately entrust the robe and the Dharma to you as the Sixth Patriarch.

The Venerable Shenxiu inscribed a verse on formlessness on the wall of the southern corridor; the Master ordered everyone to recite it and to cultivate according to this verse, so that they might avoid falling into the evil realms.
To cultivate according to this verse brings great benefit.
Huìnéng said, "Master,
I too wish to recite this single volume to establish karmic conditions for future lives!
For more than eight months while treading the pestle, I have never once gone before the hall."
"I hope you, Venerable Sir, will lead me to the verse so that I may prostrate before it.
The youth led him to the verse, and Huineng said, "I, Huineng, am illiterate;
I beg you, Venerable Sir, to read it for me."
At that time, there was a Vice Governor of Jiangzhou named Zhang Riyong, who read it aloud.
Having heard it, Huineng said, "I also have a verse;
I hope the Vice Governor will write it down for me."
The Vice-Governor said:
"Do you also compose verses?
This is truly rare."
Huineng said to the Vice Governor:
"If you wish to study unsurpassed Bodhi, you must not look down upon beginners.
Those of the lowest capacity may possess the highest wisdom, while those of the highest capacity may lack the wisdom of intent."
"If one treats others with contempt, there will be immeasurable and boundless transgressions.
The Regional Inspector said, "You simply recite the verses; I shall write them down for you."
"If you attain the Dharma, you must deliver me first.
Do not forget these words.
Huineng then spoke this verse:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; / The bright mirror is not a stand.
/ Originally there is not a single thing; / Where can dust and grime settle?
Having written this verse, the entire assembly was struck with amazement; none failed to express their wonder, and they said to one another:
"How extraordinary!
One cannot judge a person by their appearance. How could it have been so long before he caused another to become an incarnate Bodhisattva?
Seeing that the crowd was filled with wonder and apprehension, fearing they might cause him harm, the Patriarch then wiped his shoes and recited this verse:
"Furthermore, you have not yet seen your nature.
The assembly agreed with this.
On the following day, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-pounding shed and saw Huineng waist-tied with a stone, pounding rice. He said to him:
"One who seeks the Way forgets their own body for the sake of the Dharma;
should it not be thus! He then asked:
"Is the rice cooked yet?"
Huìnéng replied, "The rice has been cooked for a long time; it only lacks the final sifting.
The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff and departed.
Huìnéng immediately understood the Patriarch’s meaning and entered the inner chamber at the third watch;
the Patriarch surrounded him with his *kāṣāya* so that no one could see them, and for him he expounded the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the words, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything," Huineng attained great enlightenment at that moment, realizing that all dharmas do not depart from one's own nature.
He then addressed the Patriarch, saying:
"How unexpected it is that my own nature is fundamentally pure!"
How unexpected it is that the self-nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing;
how unexpected it is that the self-nature is fundamentally and spontaneously complete;
how unexpected it is that the self-nature is fundamentally without movement or fluctuation.
"How unexpected that this self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas!
The Patriarch, knowing that [Huìnéng] had awakened to his original nature, said to Huìnéng:
"If you do not recognize your own original mind, there is no benefit in studying the Dharma."
"If one recognizes one's own original mind and perceives one's own original nature, one is then called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, and a Buddha.
Having received the Dharma during the third watch, while no one else knew, he transmitted the Sudden Teaching along with the robe and bowl, saying:
"You are the sixth patriarch. Guard and cherish it well; deliver sentient beings extensively; propagate it for the future so that it shall never be severed."
Listen to my verse:
“When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises according to the ground.
Since insentient things have no seeds, They lack nature and thus have no arising.”
The Patriarch spoke again:

"In the past, when the Great Master Bodhidharma first came to this land, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted this robe as a physical token of faith to be inherited from generation to generation.
As for the Dharma, it is transmitted mind-to-mind, so that all may attain self-awakening and self-understanding."
"Since antiquity, Buddha after Buddha has transmitted only the fundamental essence, and master after master has secretly entrusted only the fundamental mind.
Because the robe became a cause for contention, I have stopped you and told you not to transmit it.
If you transmit this robe, your life will be like a thread hanging by a thread."
"You must depart quickly; I fear that people will harm you.
Huineng replied, "Where shall I go?"
The Patriarch said, "When you encounter Hui, stop; when you meet Hui, hide.
At the third watch, Huineng received the robe and bowl and said:
Neng said, "I am originally a man from the south and have never known these mountain paths; how shall I get out to the river mouth?
The Fifth Patriarch said, "You need not worry; I myself will escort you."
The Patriarch accompanied him for some distance until they reached Jiujiang Station.
The Patriarch ordered him to board the boat, while the Fifth Patriarch himself took up the oars and rowed. Huineng said:
"Please, Preceptor, sit;
your disciple shall take up the oars.
The Patriarch said:
"Then I shall ferry you across," [the Master] said.
Huineng replied, "When one is deluded, the teacher ferries one across; once enlightenment is attained, one ferries oneself."
Although the name "deliverance" (tú) is one, its applications differ.

I, Huineng, was born in a remote region where my speech was not standard; yet, having received the transmission of the Dharma from you, Master, I have now attained awakening. It is only fitting that I deliver myself by means of my own nature.
The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is! Hereafter,
the Buddha-dharma shall be widely propagated by you."
"You shall depart three years from now, and only then shall I pass away.
Go now with diligence toward the south;
do not speak of this too soon, for the Buddha-dharma is difficult to establish."
After Huineng had taken his leave of the Patriarch and set out for the south, he reached Mount Dayu within two months.
During these days, the Fifth Patriarch did not ascend the hall for several days.
The assembly was filled with doubt and went to inquire, saying,
"Venerable Master, are you free from illness and affliction? He replied:
"The illness has vanished.
The Dharma of the robe has already gone south. He asked:
"Who transmitted this? He replied,
"Those who are capable obtain it."
The assembly then learned of this.
Several hundred people followed in pursuit, intending to seize his robes and bowl.
There was a monk of secular surname Chen named Huiming, who had previously been a Fourth-Rank General; he was coarse and blunt by nature, yet he sought [the Master] with the utmost determination.
He went ahead of the crowd, catching up with Huineng.
Huineng threw down his robe and bowl upon a rock and said, "This robe represents the seal of faith; can it be contested by force?"
He was able to hide himself within the thickets.
When Huiming arrived, he tried to lift him up but could not move him, so he called out, "Attendant!"
"O practitioner!
I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of robes.
Huineng then went out and sat upon a flat rock.
Huiming prostrated himself and said,
