Huìnéng said, "At this very moment,
when you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, who is it that is the original face of Elder Míng?
Upon these words, Huìmíng attained great enlightenment.
He asked again,
"Apart from the secret words and secret meanings mentioned above, are there further secret meanings? Huineng replied:
"What I have spoken to you is not, in fact, secret.
If you reflect back upon yourself, the secret is right there with you. Ming said:
"Although Huiming was at Huangmei, he truly had not yet realized his own original face.
Now that I have received your instruction, it is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself."
"The practitioner here is none other than Master Huiming.
Huineng said, "If it is so, then we shall have shared the same teacher at Huangmei; take good care of yourself."
Hui Ming asked again,
"Where will you go from now on, Master Hui Neng?
Hui Neng replied:
"When we meet Yuan, we shall stop; when we encounter Meng, we shall dwell.
Mingli Ci returned to the foot of the ridge and said to his followers, "We have climbed the steep heights before, yet found no trace; we should seek them by another path."
The crowd all agreed with this.
Later, Huiming changed his name to Daoming to avoid the first character of his Master’s name.
Subsequently, when Huineng arrived at Caoxi, he was again pursued by malicious people.
He then stayed among a band of hunters during the four seasonal assemblies for a total of fifteen years, occasionally preaching the Dharma to them as appropriate.
The hunters often employed him to guard their nets, yet whenever he saw living beings caught therein, he would release them all.
Every time it was mealtime, he would put his vegetables into the meat pot to cook with them.
If someone asked about this, he would reply,
"Just eat the vegetables from the edge of the meat."
One day he reflected: "The time has come to propagate the Dharma; I must not remain in perpetual seclusion.
He then departed for Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, where he encountered Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At that time, the wind blew and the banner moved; one monk said,
"The wind moves," while another monk said:
"The banner moves.
As the debate continued without end,
Huineng stepped forward and said:
"It is not the wind that moves, nor is it the banner that moves; it is your mind, O virtuous one, that moves.
The entire assembly was struck with awe.
Yinzong invited him to the seat of honor and interrogated him on the profound meanings of the Dharma.
Seeing that Huineng’s words were concise yet profound in principle and did not rely on written texts, Huizong said:
"This practitioner is certainly no ordinary person.
I have long heard that the robe and Dharma of Huangmei have come south; could you be the one?"
Huìnéng replied, "I dare not. Thereupon,
Huìzōng performed a prostration and requested that the transmitted robe and bowl be brought forth to be displayed for the assembly.
Zongfu asked again,
"Regarding the entrustment at Huangmei, how were you instructed? Huineng replied:
"Instruction is immediately absent;
we only discuss the seeing of nature, not meditative concentration or liberation. Zong said:
"Why do you not discuss meditative concentration and liberation?
Neng replied, "These two dharmas are worldly; they are not the Buddha-dharma."
"The Buddha-dharma is the dharma of non-duality.
Zong asked again:
"What is the Buddha-dharma of non-duality?"
Huìnéng said: "The Dharma Master preaches the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and elucidates Buddha-nature; this is the non-dual dharma of the Buddha's teachings.
As the Bodhisattva Mahārājādhirāja addressed the Buddha, saying:"

"Regarding those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who have perpetrated the five heinous crimes, and those such as the icchantikas— who sever their roots of goodness— do they still possess the Buddha-nature? The Buddha said,
"There are two kinds of roots of goodness:"
First is permanence, second is impermanence; the Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent, and for this reason it is uninterrupted—this is called non-duality.
First is goodness, second is non-goodness; the Buddha-nature is neither good nor non-good—this is called non-duality.

"Regarding the aggregates (skandhas) and the elements (dhātus), ordinary people perceive them as dual; the wise, however, realize that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is itself Buddha-nature.
Upon hearing these words, Yinzong joyfully joined his palms and said, "My own lectures on the sutras have been like mere rubble."
"Your discourse on the Dharma, O Benevolent One, is like pure gold.
Thereupon, he shaved Huineng’s hair, vowing to serve him as his teacher.
Huineng subsequently established the Dongshan Dharma Gate beneath the Bodhi tree.
"Huineng obtained the Dharma at East Mountain; I endured bitter hardships until my life hung by a thread.

That I am able today to join this assembly with you, Governor, officials, monks, nuns, and laypeople—both clergy and laity—is surely due to the karmic conditions accumulated over many kalpas. It is also because in past lives we made offerings to the Buddhas and planted roots of goodness together that we have now finally been able to hear this aforementioned teaching of Sudden Enlightenment and receive the Dharma."
The teachings are those transmitted by the sages of antiquity; they are not my own wisdom, O Huineng.

Those who wish to hear the teachings of the sages of antiquity should each purify their minds; once you have heard them, each of you shall dispel your doubts, becoming no different from the sages of former generations.
The entire assembly, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced, paid their respects, and withdrew.
On the second day of the second month, Wei, the Prefectural Magistrate, requested further instruction.
The Master ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
"All of you, with pure minds, recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
He spoke again:
"Virtuous friend!
The wisdom of bodhi-prajñā is inherently possessed by all people of the world;
it is only because their minds are deluded that they cannot awaken to it themselves. They must rely upon a great virtuous friend to provide guidance and lead them to see their own nature."

"You should know that for both the foolish and the wise, the Buddha-nature is fundamentally without distinction; it is only because of their differing states of delusion and awakening that there is 'foolishness' and 'wisdom.
I shall now expound for you the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, so that each of you may individually attain wisdom."
Listen with a sincere mind!
I shall speak for you,
O Good Friend!
People spend their entire lives reciting the Prajñā with their mouths, yet they do not recognize the Prajñā of their own nature; this is like speaking of food without being satisfied by it.
If the mouth merely speaks of emptiness, one will not perceive one's nature for ten thousand kalpas, and in the end, it will be of no benefit.
"Good friend! Mahāprajñāpāramitā is a term from the Sanskrit language; it means 'Great Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore.
This must be practiced with the mind; it does not reside in verbal recitation."
If one recites with the mouth but does not practice with the mind, it is like an illusion, a transformation, dew, or lightning;
if one recites with the mouth and practices with the mind, then mind and mouth correspond. One's original nature is the Buddha; apart from this nature, there is no other Buddha.
What is meant by "Mahā"? Mahā means great.

The measure of the mind is vast and expansive, like empty space; it has no boundaries, nor does it have squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness. It is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it has no up or down, long or short. It is without anger and without joy, without right and without wrong, without good and without evil, and it has neither beginning nor end.
All Buddha-lands are entirely identical to empty space.
The wondrous nature of worldly beings is fundamentally empty; not a single dharma can be apprehended.
The true emptiness of self-nature is likewise so.
"Good friends! Do not hear my teaching on emptiness and immediately become attached to emptiness.
Above all, do not be attached to emptiness; if you sit in meditation with an empty mind, you will become attached to the emptiness of the indeterminate."

"Good friend! The world and empty space can contain the forms and images of all things: the sun, moon, and stars; mountains, rivers, and the great earth; springs, sources, streams, and ravines; grasses, trees, and forests; evil people and good people; unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas; heavens and hells; all the great oceans, Mount Sumeru, and all other mountains—all are contained within space."
The emptiness of the nature of worldly people is also like this.
Good friends! The self-nature is great because it contains all phenomena; all phenomena reside within the nature of people.
If one perceives all people—whether evil or good—and neither grasps nor rejects them, remaining unstained by attachment with a mind like space, this is called "Great"; therefore, it is termed *mahā*.
"Good friends! The deluded speak with their mouths; the wise practice with their minds.
Furthermore, there are those who are deluded who sit in empty stillness with no thoughts at all, yet claim for themselves to be great."
This class of people cannot be spoken with, because they hold false views. Good friend!
The scope of the mind is vast and great, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; when it functions, it is clear and distinct, and through its application, one immediately knows all things.
All is one, and one is all. Coming and going with freedom, the essence of mind being unimpeded—this is Prajñā.
Good friends!
All wisdom of prajñā arises from one’s own nature and does not enter from without.
Do not err in your application of the mind; this is called the true nature functioning spontaneously. When one is true, all is true.
The matter of the Mind-Only is a great undertaking; one must not practice the petty path.

Do not spend your whole day speaking of emptiness with your mouth while failing to cultivate this practice in your heart; it would be like an ordinary person claiming to be a king—this can never be achieved, and such a person is not my disciple.
"Virtuous friend! What is called *prajñā*?
*Prajñā* is, in the language of Tang, 'wisdom' (*hui*)."
In all places and at all times, to be free from delusion in every thought-moment and to constantly practice wisdom is the practice of Prajñā.
A single moment of delusion severs Prajñā; a single moment of wisdom gives rise to Prajñā.
The people of the world are deluded and do not see Prajñā; though they speak of Prajñā with their mouths, their minds remain constantly ignorant.
They often say of themselves:
"I am practicing Prajñā."
"To speak of emptiness at every thought, yet fail to recognize true emptiness—Prajñā has no form or characteristics; the mind of wisdom itself is it.
If one understands it in this way, that is what is called Prajñā-wisdom."
What is meant by *pāramitā*?
This is a term from the Western lands; in the language of Tang, it means "reaching the other shore. To explain its meaning: it is to be free from arising and ceasing.
When one clings to objects and arising and ceasing arise—like waves upon water—that is called "this shore."
Detached from objects, there is neither arising nor ceasing; like water constantly flowing through, this is called the "other shore," and is thus termed *pāramitā*.
Good friends! When those who are deluded recite these words, at the very moment of recitation, there is still delusion and error.
If one acts in every thought-moment, this is called true nature.
One who awakens to this dharma is practicing the dharma of prajñā;
one who cultivates this practice is performing the practice of prajñā.
Failure to practice is to remain an ordinary person;
to practice for even a single thought-moment, one's own body becomes equal to the Buddha. Good friends!
Ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas; afflictions are themselves Bodhi.
When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha.
When the preceding thought clings to objects, it is affliction; when the succeeding thought is detached from objects, it is Bodhi.

“Good friend! The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the most honored, the most supreme, and the foremost; it is without abiding, without going, and without coming. From within it, the Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge.”
One should employ great wisdom to shatter the afflictions and defilements of the five aggregates.
By practicing in this manner, one will certainly attain the Buddha-way, transforming the three poisons into precept, concentration, and wisdom.
"O virtuous friend!
This Dharma-gate of mine gives rise to eighty-four thousand wisdoms from a single prajñā. Why is this?"
Sentient beings of the world have eighty-four thousand afflictions.
If there were no afflictions, wisdom would be constantly manifest, never departing from its own nature.
One who awakens to this Dharma is one of non-thought, without recollection or attachment, and does not give rise to deception or falsehood.
By employing one's own true suchness-nature and observing with wisdom, neither grasping nor rejecting any phenomena—this is precisely seeing one's nature and attaining the Buddha-way.
Good friends!

If one wishes to enter the profound Dharma-realm and the samādhi of Prajñā, one must cultivate the practice of Prajñā and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; thereby, one will immediately attain the realization of one's nature.
One should know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; though it is clearly praised within the scripture, it cannot be fully described.
This Dharma-gate is the Supreme Vehicle, taught for those of great wisdom and for those of superior faculties.
When those of inferior faculties and limited wisdom hear this, they give rise to disbelief.
Why is this? It is like a great dragon sending down rain upon Jambudvīpa, where cities, towns, and villages are all swept away as if they were dates floating on a leaf.
If it rains upon the great ocean, it neither increases nor decreases.
So too, whether they be followers of the Mahāyāna or those of the Supreme Vehicle, when they hear the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, their minds open and they attain awakening.

Therefore, know that the original nature inherently possesses the wisdom of *prajñā*; because one naturally employs this wisdom to constantly observe and illuminate, there is no need for written words.

It is like rainwater, which does not originate from the heavens, but is originally brought forth by dragons, causing all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, and everything animate or inanimate, to receive its nourishment.
The myriad streams of the hundred rivers flow back into the great ocean, merging into a single body.
The nature of the original wisdom of *prajñā* within all sentient beings is likewise so.
O Good Friends!

Those of inferior faculties, upon hearing this teaching of sudden enlightenment, are like plants and trees with small root-natures; when struck by heavy rain, they all topple over of their own accord and cannot grow.
Those of inferior capacity are likewise so.
Originally, they possess the wisdom of prajñā no different from those of great wisdom; for what reason, then, do they not attain self-awakening upon hearing the Dharma?
This is because the obstacles of wrong views are heavy and the roots of affliction are deep.
It is like a great cloud covering the sun; if it is not blown away by the wind, the sunlight will not appear.

The wisdom of Prajñā has neither great nor small aspects; it is because the delusion or enlightenment of the minds of all sentient beings differs that they perceive externally due to their deluded minds, practicing in order to seek a Buddha.
As long as one has not awakened to one's own nature, this constitutes having inferior faculties.

If one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, one need not engage in external cultivation; rather, by constantly giving rise to right view within one's own mind, such that the afflictions and worldly toils can never stain it, this is precisely the realization of one's nature.
"Good friend! Not dwelling internally or externally, coming and going with freedom, able to eliminate the grasping mind, and penetrating all things without obstruction—
one who can practice this way is fundamentally no different from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
“Good friend! All sutras and written characters, the two vehicles of Great and Small, and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, are all established on account of people.”
It is only through the nature of wisdom that [the world] can be established.
If there were no people in the world, all phenomena would inherently not exist; therefore, we know that all phenomena originally arise from people.
All scriptures exist because they are spoken by people.
This is due to the fact that among people there are both the foolish and the wise; the foolish are called small persons, while the wise are called great persons.
The foolish inquire of the wise, and the wise expound the Dharma for the sake of the foolish.
When a fool suddenly attains awakening and his mind opens, he is no different from a wise person. Good friends!

When there is no awakening, even a Buddha is a sentient being; when one awakens in a single thought-moment, a sentient being is a Buddha. Therefore, know that all dharmas are entirely within one's own mind.
Why not suddenly perceive the true nature of *tathatā* within your own mind?
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:
"My original self-nature is fundamentally pure; if one recognizes one's own mind and perceives this nature, all shall attain the Buddha-way."
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
"At that moment, there was a sudden breakthrough, and he regained his original mind.
O virtuous friends!
Under my Preceptor Ren, upon hearing his words but once, I attained enlightenment and suddenly beheld the true nature of *tathatā*.
Therefore, I shall circulate this teaching to enable those who study the Way to attain sudden awakening to *bodhi*.
Each person should observe their own mind to personally realize their original nature.

If one does not awaken on one's own, it is necessary to seek a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who understands the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle (anuttarayāna) to directly point out the correct path.
These spiritual friends possess great causal conditions; that is to say, they transform and guide others so that they may realize their true nature.
All wholesome dharmas are able to be initiated because of spiritual friends.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are inherently possessed within the nature of human beings.
If one cannot awaken to this oneself, one must seek out a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for instruction before they can be seen;
if one awakens to it oneself, there is no need to seek it externally.
If one were to hold the one-sided view that liberation can only be attained through an external spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), such a thing is impossible.
Why? Because within one's own mind there is a spiritual friend by which one awakens to oneself.
If one gives rise to false delusions and inverted thoughts, even if external spiritual friends provide instruction, they cannot save one.
If one gives rise to the correct and true contemplation of Prajñā, in a single kṣaṇa, all deluded thoughts are extinguished.
If one realizes the intrinsic nature of consciousness, a single awakening brings one immediately to the stage of Buddhahood.
Good friend! When wisdom contemplates and illuminates, both internally and externally, it becomes transparently clear, and one recognizes the original mind of consciousness itself.
If one recognizes the original mind, that is primordial liberation.
If one attains liberation, that is the samādhi of prajñā, which is non-thought.
What is meant by non-thought?
If one perceives all phenomena with a mind free from attachment, this is called non-thought.
Its function pervades all places, yet it does not cling to any place.

Simply purify the fundamental mind so that the six consciousnesses emerge through the six gates; within the six sense objects, remain unstained and unmixed, coming and going with freedom, functioning universally without obstruction—this is the samādhi of prajñā, liberation through mastery, and is called the practice of non-thought.
If one does not think of any of the hundred things and causes all thoughts to cease, this is itself a bondage to the Dharma and is called an extreme view.
O Good Friends!
One who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought penetrates all dharmas completely.
"One who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought beholds the realm of all Buddhas;
one who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought attains the stage of Buddhahood. O Good Friends!"
Those in future generations who attain my Dharma shall take this sudden teaching and, toward those of like vision and practice, make a vow to uphold it as if serving the Buddha;
those who do not regress for the duration of their lives will certainly enter the ranks of the sages.
However, the transmission must follow the silent succession handed down from of old; one must not conceal the True Dharma.
If someone does not share the same view or practice and belongs to a different teaching, it must not be transmitted to them.
To harm that person brings no ultimate benefit;
fearing that foolish people might not understand and would instead slander this Dharma-gate, they would sever the Buddha-nature for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
"Good friends!
I have a verse on formlessness that you must each memorize. Whether you are laypeople or monastics, you should practice solely according to this.
If you do not practice for yourselves but merely remember my words, there will be no benefit."
Listen to my verse:
"The penetration of words and the penetration of mind Are like the sun abiding in the void.
Transmitting only the Dharma of seeing one's nature, It transcends the world and shatters heterodox schools."
The Dharma itself has neither sudden nor gradual [attainment]; it is only in the confusion and enlightenment of beings that there is slowness or speed.
This very gate of seeing one's nature cannot be fully grasped by the foolish.
Though explanations may be manifold, when they accord with principle, they all return to the One.
Within the dark abode of afflictions, one must constantly give rise to the sun of wisdom.
When the false comes, afflictions arrive; when the correct comes, afflictions are removed.
When neither the false nor the correct is employed, purity reaches its ultimate limit.
Awakening is the fundamental nature; to give rise to a [discursive] mind is itself delusion.
When the pure mind dwells amidst delusion, simply maintain correctness and there will be no three obstructions.
If people of the world cultivate the Way, nothing whatsoever shall hinder them.
Constantly seeing one's own faults, one is immediately in accord with the Way.
Within the various classes of beings there is naturally the Way; each does not obstruct or vex another.
To leave the Way and seek the Way elsewhere, one will not see the Way for the rest of one's life.
Throughout one's entire life, one may wander in vain; at the end, one will only regret it.
If you wish to perceive the True Way, practicing what is right is itself the Way.
If you yourself lack the mind for the Way, you will walk in darkness and fail to see the Way.
If one is a true practitioner of the Way, they do not see the faults of the world.
If they see the wrongs of others, their own wrongs are indeed perverse;
"the other's fault is not my fault"—if I claim this, I myself have a fault.
Simply withdraw your own sense of right and wrong, Strike down and eliminate afflictions;
With neither hatred nor love weighing on your mind, Lie down and stretch out your two legs.
If you wish to transform others, You must first possess skillful means yourself.
Do not allow them to harbor doubt; this is simply the manifestation of self-nature.
The Buddha-dharma exists within the world and is not separate from worldly awakening.
To seek bodhi apart from the world is like searching for a rabbit's horn.
Right view is called supramundane; wrong view belongs to the world.
When both wrong and right are utterly cast aside, the nature of Bodhi is manifest.
This verse is of the Sudden Teaching and is also called the Great Dharma Ship.
"The deluded hear the sutra over many kalpas; the awakened realize it in a single kṣaṇa.
The Master spoke again:
"I now preach this sudden teaching at Dàfàn Temple, universally wishing that all sentient beings within the dharma-realm may see their nature and become Buddhas upon hearing these words."
At that time, Wei the Prefect, along with his officials, monastics, and laypeople, heard what the Master had said; there was none among them who did not attain realization.
They all prostrated themselves at once and sighed in admiration: "Excellent!"
"I never expected that a Buddha would appear in the world here in Lingnan!
On the first day of the third intercalary month, Prefect Wei hosted a great assembly for a vegetarian feast for the Master.
When the meal was finished, the Prefect invited the Master to ascend the seat; together with the officials, scholars, and commoners, he assumed a solemn countenance and bowed twice, saying:
"I, your disciple, have heard the Dharma preached by the Honored One, which is truly inconceivable."
"Now I have a slight doubt; I pray that you will show great compassion and explain it specifically for me.
The Master said, "If you have a doubt, ask it immediately, and I shall explain it for you."
Wei Gong said, "Is what the Master has explained not the very essence of the Great Master Bodhidharma's teaching?
The Master replied:
"Yes," the Duke said, "I,
your disciple, have heard:..."
When Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked:
"Throughout my life, I have built temples, ordained monks, practiced charity, and hosted vegetarian feasts; what merit do these deeds bring?"
Dharma replied, "In truth,
there is no merit. The disciple,
not yet having grasped this principle, requested, "I pray that the Upādhyāya will explain it for me."
The Master said:
"In truth, there is no merit; do not doubt the words of the former sage-kings.
Emperor Wu’s mind was biased, and he did not understand the True Dharma."
Building monasteries, ordaining monks, practicing charity, and providing vegetarian feasts are called "seeking blessings," but one must not mistake these blessings for merit.
Merit resides within the Dharma-body; it does not reside in the cultivation of blessings.
The Master spoke again:
"Seeing the nature is merit; equanimity is virtue.
To be free from obstruction in every thought-moment, constantly perceiving the true and wondrous functioning of one's original nature—this is called merit and virtue."
Humility within the mind is merit; practicing propriety without is virtue.
Establishing the myriad dharmas through one's own nature is merit; the essence of the mind being free from thought is virtue.
Not departing from one's own nature is merit; applying oneself without defilement is virtue.
If you seek the dharmakāya of merit and virtue, simply act in accordance with this; this is true merit.
If a person who cultivates merit does not harbor a mind of contempt and constantly practices universal respect, they will possess merit.
If one’s mind constantly holds others in low esteem and the sense of "I" remains unbroken, then one has no merit;
if one's own nature is deluded and unreal, then one has no virtue.
Because of the conceit of self and ego, one constantly looks down upon all others.
Good friend! To be without interruption in every thought-moment is merit; for the mind’s conduct to be level and upright is virtue.
Cultivating one's own nature is merit; cultivating one's own person is virtue. Good friends!
Merit and virtue must be seen within one's own nature; they are not to be sought through giving or making offerings.
"For this reason, merit (puṇya) is distinct from spiritual realization (guṇa).
Emperor Wu did not recognize the ultimate truth; it was not my Master’s fault.
The Prefect asked again:
“Your disciple has often seen monastics and laypeople recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, vowing to be reborn in the Western Land.
I beg you, Master, to explain whether or not they can indeed be reborn there;
I pray that you will dispel my doubts.”
The Master said:
"May your lordship listen well; I, Huineng, shall explain it to you.
When the World-Honored One was in the city of Śrāvastī, he spoke of the transformation through guidance from the West."
The scriptural text is clear and not far from this.

If one were to speak in terms of physical distance, it would be one hundred and eight thousand *li*; yet, in terms of what is being explained, these refer to the ten evils and eight perversions within one's own body—this is what constitutes "distance."
To speak of the distant is for those of inferior capacity; to speak of the near is for those of superior wisdom.
While there are two kinds of people, the Dharma is not of two kinds.
There are differences between delusion and awakening, and variations in the speed of insight.
Those who are deluded seek rebirth there by reciting the Buddha's name; those who have attained awakening purify their own minds.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure."
"Your Excellency is a person from the East; as long as the mind is pure, there is no sin.
Even for a person from the West, if the mind is not pure, there is still fault.
When a person from the East commits a transgression, they recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the West."
When people of the West commit transgressions, they recite the Buddha's name and pray to be reborn in some land.
These ordinary and ignorant folk do not understand their own nature and fail to recognize the pure land within their own bodies; thus, they pray for the East and pray for the West.
The realized person is the same wherever they dwell; therefore, the Buddha said:
"Wherever one dwells, there is constant peace and joy.
As long as your mind, Excellency, is free from unwholesome thoughts, the Western Land is not far from here.
If one harbors unwholesome thoughts, it will be difficult to attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha.

I now exhort you, O good friends: first eliminate the ten evils, which is equivalent to performing one hundred thousand practices; subsequently eliminate the eight deviant paths, which is equivalent to passing beyond eight thousand.
If you perceive your true nature in every thought-moment and constantly practice with impartiality and integrity, you shall behold Amitābha as quickly as a finger-snap.
If you, Excellency, simply practice the ten wholesome deeds, why need you further aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land?
If one does not cease the ten evil states of mind, what Buddha will come to welcome and invite?
If one awakens to the sudden dharma of non-arising, the Western Land is seen to be but a single moment away.
If one does not awaken to the practice of reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth, how can one reach that destination when the path is so remote?
"Huineng and all of you shall shift the Western Land in a single kṣaṇa; it will be seen before your very eyes.
Do you each wish to see it?
The assembly all prostrated themselves and said:
"If this place can be seen, why is it necessary to further aspire for rebirth there?
I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will manifest the Western Land immediately so that everyone may see it.
The Master said:
"O Great Assembly!
For worldly people, their own physical body is a city; the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. On the outside there are five gates, and within there is the gate of the mind.
The mind is the ground, and the nature is the king."
The King dwells upon the ground of the mind; where the nature is, the King is; where the nature departs, the King is gone.
Where the nature abides, the body and mind persist; where the nature departs, the body perishes.
The Buddha acts within the nature; do not seek him outside the body.
Delusion regarding one's own nature is precisely the sentient being; awakening to one's own nature is precisely the Buddha.
Compassion is Avalokiteśvara; joy and renunciation are named Śrīkṣetra. That which can purify is Śākyamuni; that which is level and upright is Amitābha.

The self and others are Mount Sumeru; greed and desire are the ocean waters; afflictions are the waves; poison and harm are the evil dragons; falsehoods are the ghosts and spirits; and worldly toil is the fish and turtles.
Greed and anger are hell; ignorance is the realm of animals.
O virtuous friend!
If you constantly practice the ten wholesome deeds, heaven will soon be reached.
When the notion of self and person is eliminated, Mount Sumeru collapses;
when greed and desire are removed, the ocean waters dry up;
when afflictions cease to exist, the waves subside.
Poisonous harm is eliminated, and fish and dragons are cut off.
From the ground of one's own mind, the enlightened nature of the Tathāgata emits a great radiance;
externally illuminating the six sense-gates with purity, it is able to shatter the various heavens of the six realms of desire.
When one illuminates within one's own nature, the three poisons are immediately eliminated;
the offenses of the hells and other realms are extinguished all at once, such that inner and outer clarity are no different from the Western Land.
Without practicing this cultivation, how could one reach that place?
When the great assembly heard these words, they clearly perceived their own nature; they all prostrated themselves and together exclaimed, "Excellent!
They cried out:
"May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm who hear this attain awakening and understanding at once."
The Master said: "Good friends!
If you wish to practice, it can be done at home as well; it does not depend on being in a monastery."
To practice while living at home is like the people of the East whose minds are good;
to fail to cultivate oneself while in a monastery is like the people of the West whose minds are evil.
If the mind is simply pure, that is the Western Land of Self-Nature.
Master Wei asked again:
"How should one practice while living at home?
I pray that you will instruct me."
The Master said:
"I shall recite a verse on signlessness for the great assembly.
If you simply practice in accordance with this, you will always dwell with me without distinction."
If one does not practice according to this, what benefit is there in shaving one's hair and leaving the household life for the sake of the Path?
The verse says:
"When the mind is level, what need is there to uphold the precepts? When conduct is straight, what use is there to cultivate dhyāna?"
Through benevolence, one filially nourishes one's parents; through righteousness, those above and below show mutual compassion;
through yielding, the honorable and the humble live in harmony; through forbearance, the multitude of evils remains silent.
If one can drill wood to produce fire, red lotuses will surely grow from the mud.
That which is bitter to the mouth is a fine medicine; that which is harsh to the ear is surely loyal counsel.
To reform one's faults gives rise to wisdom; to protect one's shortcomings is a sign of inner lack of virtue.
Benefiting others through daily conduct; enlightenment is not attained by giving money.
Bodhi is sought only within the mind; why labor to seek the profound elsewhere?
"I have heard that by practicing according to this, the Western Land is right before one's eyes.
The Master spoke again:
"O virtuous friends!..."
In all cases, you must practice according to these verses; by perceiving the self-nature of the grasping mind, you will directly attain the Buddha-way.
Time does not wait for us; everyone, disperse now, and I shall return to Caoxi.
"If anyone among the assembly has any doubts, please come forward and ask.
At that time, the provincial governors, officials, and the virtuous men and faithful women present at the assembly each attained awakening; they believed, accepted, and practiced [the teaching].
4. Samādhi and Prajñā. The Fourth Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"Virtuous friends!
This Dharma-gate of mine takes samādhi and prajñā as its foundation."
"Great assembly!
Do not be deluded by saying that concentration and wisdom are distinct.
Concentration and wisdom are of one essence; they are not two."
Concentration is the essence of wisdom, and wisdom is the function of concentration.
When one is in wisdom, concentration is present within wisdom; when one is in concentration, wisdom is present within concentration.
If one understands this principle, it constitutes the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom.
All you practitioners of the Way, do not say that concentration arises first and wisdom follows, or that wisdom arises first and concentration follows, as if they were distinct.
To hold such a view is to see phenomena as having dual characteristics;
it is to speak virtuous words with the mouth while harboring what is unwholesome in the heart.
Emptiness possesses both meditative concentration and wisdom, yet concentration and wisdom may be unequal.
If mind and speech are both wholesome and inner and outer are as one, then concentration and wisdom are equal.
Cultivating practice through self-awakening does not consist in contention.

If you dispute over priority and sequence, you are the same as those who are deluded; you do not sever the contest for victory and defeat, but instead increase the notions of self and dharma, remaining inseparable from the four marks.
Good friend! How are concentration and wisdom? What are they like?
It is like the light of a lamp:
where there is a lamp, there is light; where there is no lamp, there is darkness.
The lamp is the substance of the light, and the light is the function of the lamp.
"Though there are two names, their essence is fundamentally one.
This dharma of concentration and wisdom is likewise so.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"Good friend! As for the Samādhi of One Practice, it consists in always maintaining a single, straightforward mind while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down in all places.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:"
"An upright mind is the site of enlightenment; an upright mind is the pure land.
Do not let your mind and actions be crooked while your mouth speaks only of uprightness;
do not merely speak of the Samādhi of One Practice with your mouth while failing to practice an upright mind.
Simply practice a straightforward mind and do not harbor attachment to any phenomena.
Deluded people become attached to the marks of dharmas and cling to the "one-practice samādhi," asserting:
"Constantly sitting without moving and not giving rise to deluded thoughts is itself the one-practice samādhi."
"One who forms such an understanding is identical to an insentient thing; it is, in fact, a cause and condition for obstructing the Way. Good friend!
The Way must flow freely; why then do you allow it to stagnate?"
When the mind does not dwell upon dharmas, the Way flows unimpeded;
if the mind dwells upon dharmas,
it is called self-bondage.
If you say that sitting constantly without moving is correct, consider how Śāriputra was rebuked by Vimalakīrti while he was sitting in meditation in the forest.
Good friend! Furthermore, there are those who teach sitting to watch the mind and contemplate stillness, remaining unmoving and unarising, and from this point on applying their efforts.
Those who are deluded do not understand this, and thus they cling to it and fall into perversion.
Many are like this, teaching one another in such a manner; therefore, we know this is a great error.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"O Good Friend! The original, correct teaching has neither sudden nor gradual aspects; it is simply that human nature naturally possesses varying degrees of sharpness and dullness.
Those who are deluded practice gradually, while those who have awakened realize it suddenly."

When one recognizes one's own original mind and perceives one's own original nature, there is no distinction; it is for this reason that the provisional names of "sudden" and "gradual" are established. Good friends!
In this Dharma-gate of mine, from the time of the ancient masters down to the present, I have first established non-thought as the宗 (zong), formlessness as the體 (ti), and non-abiding as the本 (ben).
"Signlessness" means being free from signs within signs.
"Thoughtlessness" means being without thought within thought.
"Non-abiding" is the original nature of humanity.

Regarding the good and evil, the beautiful and the ugly within the world, even down to enemies and kin, and at times when speech provokes, insults, deceives, or contends, one regards them all as empty and does not contemplate retaliation or harm; in every thought-moment, one does not dwell upon these prior objects.
If the preceding thought, the present thought, and the subsequent thought continue in succession without interruption from moment to moment, this is called bondage.
If one does not dwell upon any phenomena from moment to moment, there is no bondage.
This takes non-abiding as its foundation. Good friends!
To be externally free from all marks is called the markless.
To be able to leave behind all marks is for the essence of phenomena (dharmatā) to be pure.
This takes non-mark (animitta) as its essence.
Good spiritual friend!
When the mind is not stained by any objects, it is called "non-thought.
Within one's own thoughts, one should always remain detached from all objects and not give rise to the mind toward those objects.
If one merely does not think of any phenomena and attempts to eliminate all thoughts, such that a single thought is cut off and one dies to be reborn elsewhere, this is a great error.
Let those who study the Way reflect upon this.
If one does not understand the intent of the Dharma, it may be forgivable to err oneself, but to further mislead others;
to be deluded oneself and fail to see the truth, while moreover slandering the Buddha’s sutras—for these reasons, non-thought (amūlaka-smṛti) is established as the fundamental principle.
"Good friend! Why do we establish non-thought as the fundamental principle?

It is simply because people speak of 'seeing one's nature' with their mouths; thus, deluded persons harbor thoughts regarding external objects. Upon these thoughts, false views arise, and from them all worldly afflictions and delusive imaginings are born."

In its intrinsic nature, not a single dharma can be found; if there were anything to be found, it would be a false discourse on calamity and fortune, which is itself worldly toil and heterodox view. Therefore, this Dharma-gate establishes non-thought as its fundamental principle.
"O virtuous friend!
As for 'non-existence,' what is it that does not exist?
As for 'mindfulness,' what is it that is being mindfully contemplated?"
"Non-existence" means being devoid of dualistic characteristics and free from all defiled thoughts.
"Mindfulness" means mindfulness of the original nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
True Suchness is the substance of mindfulness, and mindfulness is the function of True Suchness.
The self-nature of True Suchness gives rise to thought; it is not the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue that can think.
Because True Suchness possesses this nature, thought arises;
if True Suchness were absent, the eyes, ears, forms, and sounds would perish at that very moment.
"Good friend!

When the self-nature of True Suchness gives rise to thought, although the six sense faculties possess seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they remain unstained by the myriad objects, and the true nature is ever-sovereign."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One who can skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
5. On Seated Meditation: The Fifth Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"In this gate of seated meditation, one fundamentally does not cling to the mind, nor does one cling to purity, nor is it a state of immobility.
If one says there is clinging to the mind, the mind is fundamentally illusory; knowing that the mind is like a phantom, there is thus nothing to which one clings."
If one says that they are attached to purity, [one must understand that] the nature of humanity is inherently pure; it is only because of deluded thoughts that True Suchness (Tathatā) is obscured.
If one simply lacks discursive thought, the nature is naturally pure;
yet, if one gives rise to the mind and becomes attached to purity, one instead generates the delusion of purity.
Delusion has no location; to be attached to it is itself delusion.

Purity has no form or appearance; yet to establish a notion of pure appearance and claim it to be spiritual practice—those who harbor such a view obstruct their own original nature and become bound by purity itself.
"Good friend!
If one cultivates immovability, when seeing any person, one does not perceive that person's right or wrong, good or evil, faults or afflictions; this is the immovability of self-nature."
"Good friend! Though the body of a deluded person remains motionless,
as soon as they open their mouth, they speak of the faults, merits, strengths, and weaknesses of others, which is to turn their back on the Way."
"If one is attached to the mind or attached to purity, it immediately obstructs the Way.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"Good friends!..."
What is meant by "sitting in meditation" (zuo chan)?
Within this Dharma-gate, to be without obstruction or hindrance, with no mental activity arising toward any external objects—whether good or evil—is called "sitting" (zuò).
To internally perceive that one's own nature is immovable is called "meditation" (chán).
"Good friend! What is called meditative concentration?
To be free from external signs is dhyāna; to be undisturbed internally is samādhi."
If one clings to external appearances, the inner mind becomes disturbed;
if one remains detached from external appearances, the mind is not disturbed.
One's original nature is inherently pure and settled; it is only because of perceiving objects and contemplating them that the mind becomes disturbed.
If the mind is not disturbed when encountering various objects, this is true samādhi. Good friend!
To be free from external signs is dhyāna; to be undisturbed internally is samādhi.
To have tranquility externally and concentration internally is what constitutes dhyāna-samādhi.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla Sūtra* states:
"My original fundamental nature is inherently pure."
"Good friends! In every thought-moment, you shall personally see that your own nature is pure; you shall personally cultivate your own practice, and you shall personally realize the Buddha-way.

6. Repentance, Repentance. At the sixth session, the Great Master saw Guang, Shao, and the commoners from the four directions gathered in the mountains to listen to the Dharma. Thereupon, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Come, all you spiritual friends!
This matter must arise from within your own affairs; at all times, in every thought-moment, purify your own minds.

Cultivate your own practice and realize your own Dharma-body; see the Buddha within your own mind, and attain self-liberation through your own precepts. Only then will you achieve this without needing to come here."
Since you have come from afar to assemble here together, you all share a common affinity.

Now, each of you should kneel with your right knee on the ground; first, I shall transmit for you the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body of self-nature, and next, I shall bestow upon you the formless repentance.
The assembly knelt with their right knees on the ground.
The Master said:
"First, the fragrance of the precepts."

That which is within one's own mind—being free from non-virtue, free from evil, free from jealousy, free from greed and hatred, and free from plundering and harming—is called the fragrance of ethical discipline (*śīla-gandha*).
Second is the fragrance of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gandha*).
When one beholds various signs of good and evil environments, yet one's own mind remains undisturbed, this is called the Incense of Concentration (Samādhi).
Third is the Incense of Wisdom (Prajñā):
when the self-mind is unobstructed, one constantly uses wisdom to contemplate and illumine one’s own nature, refraining from committing any evils.

Although one cultivates various virtues, the mind remains unattached; one honors those above and cares for those below, showing compassion to the orphaned and the poor—this is called the fragrance of wisdom.
Fourth is the fragrance of liberation.
That is, when one's own mind has no object of attachment, neither contemplating the good nor contemplating the evil, being sovereign and unimpeded—this is called the fragrance of liberation.
Fifth, the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Since one's own mind has no objective support for good or evil, one must not sink into emptiness or cling to stillness; rather, one must extensively study and gain wide learning to recognize one's own original mind and penetrate the principles of all Buddhas. Blending with the light of the world to engage with sentient beings, free from the notions of self and other, one proceeds directly to Bodhi; as the true nature remains unchanging, this is called the "incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation."
"Good friends!
This fragrance perfumes each of you internally; do not seek it outwardly.
Now I bestow upon you the formless repentance, which extinguishes the offenses of the three periods of time and causes the three karmas to become pure."
"Good friends!
Each of you follow my words and say at once:
'We, the disciples, from the past thought through the present thought to the future thought—moment by moment—are not stained by delusion or confusion.'"
I now repent of all past misdeeds, ignorance, delusions, and other offenses, praying that they be entirely extinguished at once and never arise again.
May we disciples, in our past thoughts, present thoughts, and future thoughts, remain untainted by pride and deception in every single moment of mind.
I now repent of all past evil karma, such as pride and deception; may they all be extinguished at once, never to arise again.
May we disciples, from our past thoughts through our present thoughts to our future thoughts, be untainted by envy in every single moment of mind.
"I now repent of all past evil karma, jealousy, and other transgressions; may they all be extinguished at once, never to arise again. O Good Friend!
The above constitutes the formless repentance.
What is meant by "repentance" (chan)?
What is meant by "regret" (hui)?

As for "repentance" (*chan*), it means repenting one's prior transgressions. All evil karma from the past—such as the offenses of delusion, arrogance, deceit, and envy—is entirely repented of so that they shall never arise again; this is what is called "repentance."

Repentance means regretting one's subsequent transgressions; from this day forward, regarding all evil karma and the sins of folly, delusion, arrogance, deceit, and envy, one has now awakened to them and shall sever them forever, never to commit them again—this is called repentance.
Therefore, it is called "confession" (chàn-huǐ).
Ordinary people, deluded and ignorant, know only to confess their past transgressions but do not know to repent for their future faults.
Because they do not repent, past transgressions are not extinguished, and new faults continue to arise.
"If past transgressions are not extinguished and subsequent faults arise again, how can this be called repentance?
'Good friends! Having already repented, you must now, together with these good friends, make the Four Great Vows; each of you must listen attentively and with a focused mind.'"

I vow to deliver the infinite sentient beings within my own mind; I vow to sever the infinite afflictions within my own mind; I vow to study the inexhaustible Dharma-gates of my own nature; I vow to realize the supreme Buddha-way of my own nature.
"Good friends!
Does not everyone say, 'I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings'?
Speaking thus, it is certainly not Huineng who delivers them."
"Good friend!

The sentient beings within the mind—namely, the deluded and perverse mind, the deceitful and false mind, the unwholesome mind, the envious mind, and the malicious and poisonous mind—all such minds as these are entirely sentient beings."
Each must deliver oneself by means of one's own nature; this is called true deliverance.
What is meant by "delivering oneself by means of one's own nature"?
It is to deliver the sentient beings within one's own mind—those possessed of false views, afflictions, and ignorance—by means of right view.
Once right view is established, one employs the wisdom of *prajñā* to shatter the ignorance and delusion of sentient beings, so that each may cross over for themselves.

When the false comes, they are crossed over by the true; when confusion comes, they are crossed over by awakening; when folly comes, they are crossed over by wisdom; when evil comes, they are crossed over by goodness.
To cross over in this manner is called "true crossing."
Furthermore, regarding the vow to sever boundless afflictions: it is to employ the wisdom of one's own inherent prajñā to eliminate the mind of false conceptualization.
Moreover, regarding the vow to study inexhaustible Dharma-gates: one must personally realize one's nature and constantly practice the True Dharma; this is called true study.

Furthermore, having vowed to accomplish the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, one is constantly able to humble the mind, practicing what is truly correct; remaining free from both delusion and awakening, one constantly gives rise to prajñā.
When delusion is eliminated and truth is realized, one immediately perceives the Buddha-nature; thus, the Way of the Buddha is accomplished in an instant.
Constantly mindful of practice is the dharma of the power of aspiration. "O Good Friend!
Now that the Four Great Vows have been made, the Good Spiritual Friend shall further bestow upon you the precepts of the Three Refuges of Non-characteristic.
Good Spiritual Friend!
I take refuge in Awakening, the Honored One among the two-legged.
I take refuge in the Righteous, the Honored One who has transcended desire;
I take refuge in the Pure, the Honored One among the multitudes.

From this day forth, I shall call the Awakened One my teacher and no longer take refuge in demons, heretics, or external paths. With the Three Jewels of one's own nature constantly serving as witness, I exhort all spiritual friends to take refuge in the Three Jewels of their own nature.
"Buddha" means awakening;
"Dharma" means correctness;
"Saṅgha" means purity.

Taking refuge in the awakening of one’s own mind, so that delusion does not arise, possessing few desires and being content, and being able to remain detached from wealth and sensual pleasures—one is called the Honored One of Two Feet.

Taking refuge in the correctness of one’s own mind, with every thought free from false views, and because of the absence of false views, being devoid of the conceit of self and others, as well as greed, attachment, and clinging—one is called the Honored One Who is Free from Desire.

When one’s own mind takes refuge in purity, such that the nature of all realms of affliction and sensual desire is fundamentally unstained by attachment, one is called the Honored One among the Multitude.
To cultivate this practice is to take refuge in oneself.
Ordinary people do not know how to receive the Three Refuges from day until night.
If one says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," where is the Buddha?
If one does not see the Buddha, upon what basis can one take refuge? To speak thus would be a falsehood.
"Good friends! Observe each other and do not apply your minds erroneously.
The scriptural text clearly states that one takes refuge in the Buddha oneself; it does not say that one takes refuge in another Buddha."
Since the Buddha has not returned, there is no external place of refuge.

Now that you have attained self-awakening, each of you must take refuge in the Three Jewels within your own mind: internally harmonizing the nature of the mind and externally showing respect to others—this is true self-refuge.

“Good friends! Having already taken refuge in your own Three Jewels, each of you with a sincere mind, I shall speak to you of the Buddha of the self-nature of the three bodies as one essence, so that you may clearly perceive the three bodies and awaken to your own nature.”
Everyone followed my lead:
"In one's own physical body, take refuge in the Buddha of the Pure Dharma-body.
In one's own physical body, take refuge in the Buddha of the Perfect Reward-body."
"In one's own physical body, take refuge in the thousand, ten-thousand, and billion transformation Buddhas.
"Good friend! The physical body is a dwelling; it cannot be said to be 'refuge'."
The aforementioned three bodies of the Buddha exist within one's own nature; all worldly people possess them, yet because their own minds are deluded, they do not perceive their internal nature.
They seek the Tathāgatas of the three bodies externally, failing to see that the Buddhas of the three bodies are present within themselves.
Listen well, all of you, so that within your own bodies you may perceive the three kāya Buddhas of self-nature.
These three kāya Buddhas arise from self-nature; they are not obtained from without.
What is meant by the Buddha of the Pure Dharma-body?
The nature of worldly beings is fundamentally pure, and all phenomena arise from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
When one deliberates upon any evil matter, evil conduct immediately arises.
When one contemplates all wholesome matters, wholesome conduct arises.

Thus, these dharmas abide within their own nature; they are like the sky, which is eternally pure, or the sun and moon, which are eternally bright, yet appear bright above and dark below when shrouded by floating clouds.
Suddenly, when the wind blows and the clouds disperse, both above and below become bright, and the myriad phenomena all appear.
The nature of worldly people is constantly drifting and wandering, like those clouds in the sky.
O Good Knowledge!
Wisdom is like the sun and insight is like the moon; wisdom and insight are ever-luminous.
When one is attached to external objects, the clouds of deluded thoughts cover the self-nature, preventing it from being bright and clear.

If one encounters a virtuous friend, hears the true and correct Dharma, and personally eliminates delusion and ignorance, then both internally and externally there will be clear penetration, and all phenomena will manifest within one's own nature.
One who has seen their nature is also like this;
this is called the Buddha of the Pure Dharma-body. Good friend!
Taking refuge in the nature of one’s own mind is taking refuge in the true Buddha.

As for taking refuge in oneself: it consists in eliminating from within one's own nature all unwholesome thoughts—such as envy, deceit, pride, hypocrisy, delusion, contempt for others, arrogance toward others, wrong views, and haughtiness—as well as all unwholesome conduct at all times; constantly observing one’s own faults and not speaking of the good or evil of others—this is taking refuge in oneself.

One must always humble oneself and practice universal respect; this is the realization of the nature of reality (dharmatā) through thorough penetration, free from further obstructions—it is one's own refuge.
What is called the "Perfectly Full Reward Body" (saṃbhogakāya)?
Just as a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand years, a single moment of wisdom can extinguish the ignorance of ten thousand years.
Do not dwell on what lies ahead, for that which has already passed cannot be recovered;
always contemplate what follows, so that in every thought-moment you may become perfectly luminous and perceive your own original nature.
Although good and evil differ, their fundamental nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is called the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Within this true nature, one is unstained by good or evil; this is named the Buddha of the Perfectly Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
If from one's own nature a single thought of evil arises, it extinguishes the roots of goodness accumulated over ten thousand kalpas;
if from one's own nature a single thought of goodness arises, all evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are exhausted.
Continuing thus until reaching unsurpassed Bodhi, seeing within oneself in every moment and not losing the original thought is called the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).
What is meant by the "thousand billion transformation bodies"?
If one does not contemplate the myriad dharmas, their nature is fundamentally like space; yet, a single thought of deliberation is called "transformation.
If one deliberates on evil matters, one transforms into hell.
Contemplating wholesome matters transforms them into heavenly realms;
poison and harm transform into dragons and snakes; compassion transforms into bodhisattvas; wisdom transforms into the upper realms; and ignorance transforms into the lower regions.

The transformations of the self-nature are exceedingly manifold; deluded persons fail to awaken to them, giving rise to evil thought after thought and constantly traversing the paths of unwholesomeness.
If they turn back even a single thought toward goodness, wisdom will immediately arise; this is called the Buddha of the Self-Nature Transformation Body.
"Good friend! The Dharma-body is inherently present; when one perceives its own nature in every thought-moment, that is the Reward-body Buddha.
When one contemplates from the perspective of the Reward-body, that is the Transformation-body Buddha."
The self-realization, self-cultivation, and the merits of one's own nature are the true refuge.
Skin and flesh constitute the physical body; the physical body is merely a dwelling, and thus it is not called a refuge.
Simply by awakening to the three bodies of one's own nature, one recognizes the Buddha of one's own nature.
I have a verse on formlessness; if you can take it as your teacher and uphold it, my words shall cause the sins of your delusions accumulated over kalpas to be extinguished all at once.
The verse says:
"Deluded people cultivate merit but do not cultivate the Way; they claim that cultivating merit is itself the Way.
Though their almsgiving and offerings bring boundless merit, within their hearts they continue to commit the three evils."
If one intends to cultivate merit to extinguish transgressions, merit may be gained in future lives while transgressions remain;
simply eliminate the conditions for transgression within the mind—this is called true repentance within the self-nature.
Suddenly awakening to the true repentance of the Mahāyāna, Eliminating deviance and practicing rectitude, one is then free from transgression;
If one constantly contemplates one's own nature while studying the Way, One is immediately of the same category as all Buddhas.
My ancestors transmitted only this Sudden Dharma; may all universally wish to see their nature as one single essence.
If you desire to seek the Dharmakāya in the future, cleanse your mind of all dharmic characteristics.
Strive to see for yourself; do not be indolent. If the succeeding thought suddenly ceases, this life will come to rest.
If you awaken to the Mahāyāna and attain the seeing of your nature, Reverently join your palms and seek it with a sincere heart.
The Master said: "Good friend!
You must memorize it all and practice according to this; you shall see your nature in an instant."
"Though one be a thousand *li* away, they are as if always by my side.
If you do not awaken upon these words, then even face-to-face you are a thousand *li* apart; why then have you taken such trouble to come from afar?"
"Take care! Go well.
Upon hearing the Dharma, the entire assembly was enlightened; they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

7. Circumstances of the Encounter, Part Seven. After the Master received the Dharma from Huangmei, he returned to Cao Hou Village in Shaoguan, where no one recognized him. According to another version of the text: "When the Master departed, he went to Cao Hou Village and stayed for over nine months."
However, the Master himself said:
"In no more than thirty-odd days, I reached Huangmei.
Given his intensity in seeking the Way, how could there have been any lingering delay?
It was not correct for him to depart.
There was a Confucian scholar named Liu Zhilüe who treated him with great courtesy.
Zhilüe had an aunt who was a nun named Wujinzang, who constantly recited the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Master listened briefly and immediately understood the profound meaning, whereupon he proceeded to explain it.
The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters;
the Master said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask you to question me regarding the meaning."
The nun said, "I do not even recognize the characters; how could I possibly understand their meaning?
The Master said:
"The sublime principles of the Buddhas have no connection with written words.
The nun was struck with wonder and announced this throughout the village to the elders, saying:
"This is a man of the Way; you should invite him to receive our offerings."
Cao Shuliang, a descendant of the fourth generation of the Wei Prince Wuhou (one source says Jin), along with the local residents, vied with one another to come and pay their respects.

At that time, the ancient Bao Lin Temple had already been destroyed by the fires of war since the end of the Sui dynasty; consequently, they rebuilt the Buddhist monastery upon its old foundations and invited the Master to reside there.
In a short time, it was transformed into a precious monastery; the Master resided there for over nine months, but as he was again pursued by a faction of evildoers, he fled to the mountains ahead.
They set fire to the vegetation, but the Master escaped harm by hiding his body and pressing himself against a rock.
On this rock today there are the traces of the Master’s cross-legged sitting and the patterns of his robe; for this reason, it is named "The Rock of Seeking Refuge.
Recalling the Fifth Patriarch’s instruction to hide him away, the Master then traveled and remained in seclusion within two districts.
The monk Fahai was a native of Qujiang in Shaoyou.
When he first visited the Patriarch, he asked:
"Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' I pray that you will deign to provide further instruction."
The Master said:
"The non-arising of the preceding thought is the mind; the non-extinguishing of the succeeding thought is the Buddha.
The manifestation of all phenomena is the mind; the detachment from all phenomena is the Buddha."
If I were to explain this in full detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Listen to my verse:
"The very mind is called wisdom; The very Buddha is concentration. When concentration and wisdom are held in equal balance,"
The mind is pure within;
awaken to this Dharma-gate. Through your habitual nature, employ that which is fundamentally unborn; cultivating these two together is the correct path.
Upon hearing these words, Fahai attained great enlightenment and praised him with a verse:
"The very mind is originally the Buddha; Failing to realize this, one remains self-subdued.
I now know the causes of concentration and wisdom: Cultivating them both, one transcends all phenomena."
Sengfada was a native of Hongzhou; he entered the monastic order at the age of seven and constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
When he came to pay his respects to the Patriarch, his head did not touch the ground.
The Master rebuked him, saying:
"If you do not prostrate yourself on the ground, how is that any better than not prostrating at all?
There must be something within your mind."
"What have you been practicing?
He replied, "I have already recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* three thousand times."
The Master said:
"If you were to recite ten thousand fascicles until you grasp the meaning of the scriptures and yet did not consider that a victory, then you would walk with me.
Now you carry this burden of religious work, yet you do not recognize your own transgression."
Listen to my verse:
"Ritual is fundamentally for breaking the banner of arrogance; why then does one's head not touch the ground?
When 'self' exists, fault immediately arises; when it is absent, merit and blessings are beyond compare."
The Master asked again,
"What is your name? He replied:
“Fada,” the Master said, “your name is Fada; how have you ever truly mastered the Dharma?”
He further spoke in verse:
"You are now named Fada; you recite diligently without ceasing.
Yet you recite in vain, merely following the sounds; to clarify the mind is what is called being a Bodhisattva."
"Because you now possess the necessary conditions, I shall now speak for your sake;
simply believe that the Buddha is beyond words, and lotus flowers shall issue from my mouth.
Having heard this verse, Da repented and apologized, saying:
"From this day forward, I shall be humble toward all.
As a disciple reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I have not yet understood its meaning, and my mind is constantly filled with doubt."
"Venerable Master, your wisdom is vast and great; I pray that you will briefly explain the principles within the sutra.
The Master said, "Fada!
The Dharma is thoroughly understood, yet your mind does not understand it.

On the third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Xuantian era (the Gui-chou year), which was the twelfth month of that same year when the reign title was changed to Kaiyuan, the Great Master, having finished his midday meal at Guoen Temple, addressed his disciples, saying:

Dharma-Sea said, "Preceptor!
What teachings do you leave behind so that those who are deluded in future generations may perceive their Buddha-nature?"
The Master said: “Listen attentively!
Those deluded people of future generations—if they recognize sentient beings as being the Buddha-nature;”
If you do not recognize the sentient beings within yourself, it will be difficult to encounter a Buddha even after seeking for ten thousand kalpas.
I shall now instruct you:
recognize the sentient beings of your own mind and perceive the Buddha-nature within your own mind.
If you wish to seek and see the Buddha, recognize only sentient beings.
It is simply because sentient beings are deluded regarding the Buddha; it is not that the Buddha is deluded regarding sentient beings.
If one awakens to one's own nature, sentient beings are the Buddha.
If one is deluded regarding self-nature, a Buddha is a sentient being.
When self-nature is equal, a sentient being is a Buddha;
when self-nature is perverse and treacherous, a Buddha is a sentient being.
If your minds are treacherous and crooked, even though the Buddha is among sentient beings;
yet if for a single thought-moment you are level and upright,
then these sentient beings become Buddhas.
Within my own mind there is a Buddha; this self-Buddha is the true Buddha.
If within one's own mind there were no Buddha-mind, where could one seek the true Buddha?
You all are Buddhas within your own minds; do not harbor further doubts.
Externally there is not a single thing that can be established; all are the fundamental mind giving rise to myriad phenomena.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"When the mind arises, myriad phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, myriad phenomena cease."
"I now leave behind for you this one verse as a parting gift, titled 'The Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature.
Those of future generations who understand the meaning of this verse will perceive their own original mind and spontaneously realize the Way of the Buddha."
The verse says:
"The self-nature of True Suchness is the True Buddha; wrong views and the three poisons are the Demon King.
When one is deluded by error, the demon dwells in the house; when one possesses right view, the Buddha dwells in the hall."
When false views and the three poisons arise within one's nature, it is the Demon King who has come to dwell in one's house;
when right view spontaneously eliminates the mind of the three poisons, the demon transforms into a Buddha—truly without pretense.
The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—these three bodies are originally but one body.
If you can perceive them within your own nature, this is precisely the cause for attaining the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
The pure nature originally arises from the transformation body; The pure nature is ever-present within the transformation body.
This nature causes the transformation body to practice the right path, So that in the future it may achieve perfect and inexhaustible truth.
The nature of lust is fundamentally the cause of the pure nature; removing lust is itself the body of the pure nature.
Within this nature, each person must individually leave behind the five desires; seeing the nature in a single instant is itself the truth.
If in this life you encounter the gate of the Sudden Teaching, Suddenly awakening to your own nature, you see the World-Honored One.
If you wish to practice cultivation to seek Buddhahood, You will not know where to go to seek the Truth.
If you can see the truth within your own mind, That very truth is the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Failing to see your own nature while seeking the Buddha elsewhere, To give rise to such thoughts is to be a person of total delusion.
The Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching has now been left behind; to save and deliver the people of the world, you must cultivate it yourself.
I tell you, future seekers of the Way: if you do not form this view, you will remain in great indolence.
When the Master had finished speaking these verses, he said:

After my parinirvāṇa, do not act out of worldly sentiment by weeping and shedding tears, nor accept the condolences of others or wear mourning garments; such are neither my disciples nor the True Dharma."

Simply recognize your own original mind and see your own true nature: it is neither moving nor still, neither arising nor ceasing, neither departing nor coming, neither right nor wrong, and neither abiding nor wandering.
I fear that your minds may be deluded and fail to grasp my meaning; therefore, I now re-exhort you so that you may realize your true nature.
After my parinirvāṇa, practice according to this as if I were still in the world.
If you violate my teachings, even though I remain in the world, it will be of no benefit to you.
He further spoke in verse:

After the Master had spoken these verses, he sat upright until the third watch of the night, when he suddenly said to his disciples,

At that time, an extraordinary fragrance filled the chamber, a white rainbow stretched toward the earth, the forest trees turned white, and birds and beasts wailed in grief.

He then burned incense and prayed, saying:

The Master was seventy-six years old; he transmitted the robe at the age of twenty-four and received the tonsure at thirty-nine. In the spring of the following year, the Master took leave of the assembly to return to Baolin; more than a thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, escorted him as far as Caoxi.

The immortal said, "I know that the Dharma-power of the Monk is vast and great; however, the tombs of my high ancestors are all located here. As for that Jewel Forest Dharma-assembly site, it was also previously when the Tripitaka Master Jñānabhadra from the Western Regions, having traveled from the South Sea to the mouth of the Caoxi River, scooped up some water to drink; finding it fragrant and delicious, he marveled at its excellence.

Following the current to its source, he beheld the mountains and waters encircling one another and the peaks rising in wondrous beauty, and he sighed, saying:
"It is just like Mount Baolin in the Western Heaven," he said.
Then, addressing the residents of Cao Hou Village, he said:

"A Buddhist monastery may be established on this mountain. One hundred and seventy years from now, the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure shall be propagated here, and those who attain the Way will be as numerous as the trees in a forest; it should therefore be named 'Baolin' (Precious Forest)."

At that time, Hou Jingzhong, the Governor of Shaozhou, submitted a memorial detailing these words to the Emperor. The Emperor granted his request and bestowed the name "Baolin" (Jewel Forest) upon it; thus it became a Buddhist monastery, completed in the third year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
In front of the temple hall was a pond where a dragon frequently appeared and disappeared, striking the wooden boats and shaking the trees.
One day, it manifested its form as exceedingly massive; the waves surged violently, and clouds and mist shrouded the sky, causing all the disciples to tremble with fear.
The Master rebuked him, saying:

"You can only manifest a large body, but you cannot manifest a small body. If you were a divine dragon, you ought to be able to undergo transformations, manifesting the small through the large and the large through the small."
The dragon suddenly vanished; after a brief moment, it reappeared with a small body, leaping out from the surface of the pond.
The Master spread out his alms bowl and tested it, saying, "You do not yet dare to enter into this old monk's bowl."
The dragon then swam forward to his presence; the Master scooped it up with his alms bowl, yet the dragon could not move.
The Master carried the bowl into the hall and preached the Dharma to the dragon, whereupon the dragon shed its bones and departed.
The bone was approximately seven inches long, complete with head, tail, horns, and feet, and was preserved at the temple gate.
Later, the Master filled the pond with earth and stones; the site where an iron stupa now stands to the left of the hall's front is that very place.
